Jane is charged with two counts of murder of both her children, and here is the background of the case:
After Jane and Frank had been happily married for 5 years, their first son, Andy, was born.
When Andy was 11 weeks old, Jane found the baby had fallen unconscious after being put to bed when she was alone with the baby at home. Jane soon called an ambulance, but Andy was declared dead after being transported to the hospital. A post-mortem was conducted and it suggested natural causes of death.
After one year, Jane and Frank's second son, Ben, was born. When Ben was 8 weeks old, Jane discovered that the baby was unwell, and the couple called an ambulance. However, Ben could not be resuscitated either and was pronounced dead. An autopsy was conducted and injuries to the ribs and spinal cord, hypoxic damage (low level of oxygen) to the brain, and haemorrhages to the eyes and eyelids were discovered.
As a result of this finding, further tests based on Andy's (the first son) autopsy photographs were carried out, and found bruises to the arms and legs, a torn frenulum, and blood in the lung. Subsequently, Jane was charged with two counts of murder of both children by smothering them.
Another possible explanation for the death of Andy and Ben is sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), also known as COT or CRIB death. This is a sudden and unexplainable death of infants during their first year of life. There are a number of risk factors that correlate with SIDS, but no clear mechanism or cause has been identified. The frequency of SIDS is 1 in 4,000 in the UK, and it is more common among boys than girls.

The spinal bleeding that was found in Ben is a common finding in natural death, and the dislocated ribs probably occurred post-mortem or due to resuscitation attempts.

The similarities between both incidents are astonishing: both babies were about the same age when they died; they both died at similar time of the day after just being fed; and they were both found unconscious by Jane when she was alone with them.

If Jane is not guilty, some similarities between two infant deaths in the same family could arise naturally because siblings often share routines, feeding patterns, sleeping environments, caregiving arrangements, and age-related vulnerabilities. That said, the combination of both babies dying at a similar age, at a similar time of day, after feeding, and while alone with Jane is still a fairly notable cluster of similarities. So under the not-guilty hypothesis, I’d rate this as possible but not especially likely.

If Jane is guilty, these similarities would be quite likely, because repeated acts by the same person often occur under similar circumstances: similar victim age, similar household routine, similar timing, and the accused being alone with the child. It would not be certain, but the recurrence of a similar pattern fits the guilty hypothesis well.

If Jane is not guilty, it is still quite possible that Ben’s hypoxic brain damage was caused a matter of hours before death, because hypoxic injury can arise from natural or accidental processes before a fatal collapse. The timing of the injury does not by itself strongly distinguish guilt from innocence; it mainly speaks to when the oxygen deprivation occurred, not necessarily why.

If Jane is guilty, it is also quite plausible that the hypoxic damage to Ben’s brain was caused a matter of hours before death, since intentional smothering or other inflicted hypoxia could have produced injury before the final fatal event. Again, this timing evidence is compatible with guilt, though not uniquely so.

I can’t reliably assign a meaningful numerical probability of guilt from this summary alone. In a murder case, doing so would require a full evidential assessment, including the credibility of the medical experts, alternative explanations for each finding, the statistical dependence between the two deaths, and the legal standard of proof. A simple number here would risk overstating certainty from contested forensic evidence.

That said, based only on the evidence as presented, the case appears suspicious but far from conclusively resolved, because several findings are said to be compatible with innocent explanations while others are said to be indicative of smothering or abuse. So my overall view would be that guilt is possible and perhaps more likely than not on this limited summary, but not close to certainty.
